talks.title: Keynote | High-assurance Code Reviews: How Consulting Works When The Risks Are High by Dan Guido
talks.teaser: Evaluates keynote | High-assurance Code Reviews: How Consulting Works When The Risks Are High by Dan Guido and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Dan Guido delivers the nullcon Berlin keynote on high-assurance code reviews, comparing blockchain security challenges with traditional consulting when risks are extreme.

Key Topics: Solidity's security failures despite modern language design lessons; trailer bits consulting model changes under high risk; the desperate need for blockchain developers; and why some security problems are easier on one side of the fence.

Technical Details: Guido discusses how Solidity threw out decades of security learnings when designed for JavaScript developers, creating a language only a few years old with vulnerabilities that took C++ 40 years to accumulate.

Takeaways: High-assurance environments demand different consulting approaches than typical engagements. New technology stacks like blockchain often repeat security mistakes that mature languages solved decades ago.

talks.title: Night Track | GNU Anastasis: Privacy-Preserving Key Backup And Recovery by Christian Grothoff
talks.teaser: Explores night Track | GNU Anastasis: Privacy-Preserving Key Backup And Recovery by Christian Grothoff and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Problem With Classic Secret Sharing

Christian Grothoff presents GNU Anastasis for privacy-preserving key backup and recovery without a trusted third party. Shamir k-of-n sharing solves confidentiality but not usability—recovery should not require coordinating many friends or providers for practical key sizes.

Provider-Based Recovery Design

Anastasis splits secrets across independent service providers who learn almost nothing about users. The client derives a user ID by hashing sensitive personal attributes locally (never stored in cleartext), then encrypts key shares with derived keys K1 and K2. Providers store encrypted blobs plus recovery challenges encrypted under K2.

Recovery Flow and Adversary Models

Recovery recomputes identifiers and K2, selects providers, completes per-provider challenges (email, SMS, security questions), decrypts enough shares with K1, and reconstructs the secret on-device. Weak adversaries lack full identity data; strong adversaries who know identifiers must coerce multiple jurisdictions/providers. Per-provider salted identifiers and configurable boolean recovery policies add flexibility beyond simple threshold schemes.

talks.title: Fuzzware: Automating & Scaling Fuzzing For Firmware by Tobias Scharnowski & Marius Muench | Nullcon
talks.teaser: Outlines fuzzware: Automating & Scaling Fuzzing For Firmware by Tobias Scharnowski & Marius Muench | Nullcon and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Firmware Beyond Linux Routers

Tobias Scharnowski presents Fuzzware, a framework for automated rehosting and fuzzing of embedded firmware ranging from PLCs and ECUs to IoT appliances. Many devices lack Linux shells, making traditional on-device fuzzers impractical and physically risky—one audience member reportedly overheated a router during fuzzing.

Hardware Interaction Primitives

Bare-metal firmware communicates via memory-mapped I/O, interrupts, and DMA rather than file descriptors. A simple getchar on serial may touch multiple MMIO registers, complicating input injection for fuzzers accustomed to stdin and syscalls.

Rehosting in the Cloud

Fuzzware automatically builds virtual execution environments that emulate peripherals so firmware can run on general-purpose systems. Cloud-scale deployment accelerates campaigns that would be slow or destructive on physical hardware, aligning with prior sessions on making systems fuzz-friendly.

Pipeline Overview

The workflow ingests firmware binaries, models MMIO and interrupt behavior, and feeds mutated inputs through rehosted images to find crashes. Scharnowski positions Fuzzware as infrastructure for scaling firmware security research across diverse embedded targets beyond consumer Wi-Fi routers.

talks.title: CXO Panel | Digital Identity In The Age Of Fintech | Nullcon Berlin 2022
talks.teaser: Explores CXO Panel | Digital Identity In The Age Of Fintech | Nullcon Berlin 2022 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Fintech identity landscape

Moderator Benoit Flippen (CISO, Scout24) convenes leaders from Solarisbank, Nuri, FINRA, and other fintechs to discuss digital identity challenges beyond banking APIs. Panelists describe embedding financial services in third-party products, fast growth, and regulatory pressure on access management.

Org models for IAM

Companies split customer-facing trust-and-safety flows from internal IAM. Scout24 places IAM engineering inside the information security group while tech ops handles day-to-day operations. FINRA's second-line security team defines access requirements; first-line asset owners implement them under periodic review mandates.

Regulatory access reviews

German and EU financial rules require regular access recertification—administrative privileges reviewed at least twice yearly. Panelists stress that scaling IAM in hypergrowth fintechs means documenting default developer permissions, escalation paths, and audit evidence, not just deploying SSO.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Moderated by Benoit Philippart, this executive panel at Nullcon Berlin 2022 brings together chief security officers from leading European FinTechs, digital banks, and crypto-custodians—including Solarisbank, N26, Nuri, and Finoa. The panel explores the intricate challenges of architecting robust digital identity and access management (IAM) across rapidly evolving financial services. The discussion navigates the friction between stringent regulatory mandates, scalable customer onboarding, fraud mitigation, and emerging decentralized identity paradigms.

Key Topics:
- Core IAM architectures across Banking-as-a-Service (BaaS), retail banking, and crypto custody.
- Regulatory compliance drivers: PSD2, Strong Customer Authentication (SCA), KYC/AML, and eIDAS.
- Separation and governance of internal enterprise identity versus customer-facing authentication.
- Decentralized identity frameworks versus centralized identity provider honeypots.

Technical Details:
The panelists dissect the operational realities of securing digital identities within regulated financial ecosystems. Guido Heissmann of Solarisbank emphasizes that as a Banking-as-a-Service infrastructure provider, the platform must decouple internal corporate IAM from tenant-facing customer authentication while enforcing rigorous threat modeling across cross-functional engineering and dedicated trust-and-safety teams. Travis Kerlock of N26 highlights the practical impact of the Revised Payment Services Directive (PSD2) and its Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) mandates. Financial institutions are legally obligated to expose open banking APIs to third-party providers, requiring resilient authorization flows that bind user identity to registered mobile devices and multi-factor primitives while balancing merchant fraud delegation.

In the cryptocurrency and investment sector, Alessandro of Nuri and Sheetal of Finoa detail the heightened stakes associated with digital asset custody, where identity compromise leads to irreversible financial loss. The panel debates the structural tension between centralized identity verification systems and decentralized alternatives such as eIDAS-compliant digital identities and self-sovereign identity models. Centralized databases create massive single points of failure that attract targeted adversary intrusion, while distributed models shift operational complexity and recovery burdens directly onto end users and relying parties.

Technical infrastructure scalability is examined as a critical facet of identity system security. In crypto and FinTech platforms, extreme market volatility frequently induces sudden order-of-magnitude spikes in authentication traffic—such as tens of thousands of users logging in concurrently within minutes. The panelists explain how session synchronization, distributed token validation, and token revocation across microservice architectures must be architected to withstand these surges without degrading security postures or exposing race conditions in authorization logic.

Key Takeaways:
Digital identity serves as the fundamental perimeter in modern FinTech, requiring continuous threat modeling and rigorous separation between internal workforce access and consumer authentication pipelines. Organizations must design architectures capable of complying with evolving European regulatory directives like PSD2 and eIDAS without sacrificing API performance or user experience. Security teams must ensure authentication infrastructure can scale dynamically under severe market traffic spikes while deploying robust session management to prevent token misuse and credential stuffing attacks.

talks.title: Making Of: The Sanitizer API by Frederik Braun | Nullcon Berlin
talks.teaser: Outlines making Of: The Sanitizer API by Frederik Braun | Nullcon Berlin and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
```json
{
  "summary": "Overview

Frederik Braun, Staff Security Engineer at Mozilla, presents the Sanitizer API—a proposed W3C incubator group specification with prototype implementations in Chrome and Firefox designed to address DOM-based cross-site scripting vulnerabilities. Despite being a well-understood problem, XSS remains the most reported security vulnerability for over a decade, particularly in single-page applications and Electron-based software.

Key Topics

1. DOM-Based XSS Problem
The fundamental vulnerability is simple: `element.innerHTML = attacker_controlled_string`. Braun traces his experience fixing XSS issues in Firefox UI and generalizing solutions for web applications, observing three common fix approaches: using text content instead of HTML, attempted encoding/escaping (often unsuccessful), and dealing with intertwined template and user input. He argues most could be fixed with a proper sanitizer.

2. Initial Design & Critical Pitfalls
The first API design used parse-sanitize-serialize steps returning a string. However, this created double parsing: the sanitizer would parse and serialize to a string, then `innerHTML` would parse again. This causes MXSS (mutation XSS) vulnerabilities where subtle parsing differences between contexts allow attacker bypass.

Technical Details

1. Fragment Parser Context Problem
A critical insight from the HTML specification: two parsing algorithms exist. The document parser handles full HTML documents (used when loading pages), while the fragment parser handles partial HTML snippets (used by `innerHTML`) and crucially requires a context element. Different HTML elements have different parsing rules—table elements parse radically differently depending on context. The initial implementation incorrectly assumed a body context, failing for tables, select elements, and other context-sensitive elements.

2. Sanitizer Bypass via Parsing Mismatch
Security researcher Michael Benkowski reported a bypass: SVG content with nested HTML elements serialized one way through the fragment parser but differently through the document parser (used for iframe src assignment), bypassing sanitization and enabling XSS.

3. Current Solution: setHTML() API
The solution integrates parsing, sanitization, and DOM insertion into a single operation:
```
element.setHTML(input, {sanitizer: config})
```
This uses the fragment parser with the correct context element, sanitizes the resulting tree, and appends it to the DOM atomically—preventing double parsing entirely. Alternative methods include `sanitize()` returning a document fragment and discouraged `sanitizeToString()` for strings.

Security Scope & Limitations

Server-side XSS is out of scope; the API focuses on client-side DOM-based vulnerabilities. Three known attack classes require consideration:

1. DOM Clobbering: Injected elements confuse JavaScript by shadowing real properties. Mitigatable by configuring the sanitizer to remove name and id attributes.

2. Script Gadgets: Framework-specific XSS via template syntax or library behavior. Universal prevention is impossible, but frameworks can configure their own sanitizers.

3. MXSS: Remains vulnerable if code re-parses output afterward. Single parsing in the Sanitizer API mitigates this but does not completely solve it if developers parse again.

Design Principles

- Safe by default: No configuration enables XSS; the API guarantees safety
- Responsibility shift: XSS via Sanitizer API becomes a browser bug, not developer responsibility
- Reuses browser parser: Future-proof against HTML syntax changes; avoids mismatches that plague external sanitizer libraries
- Configurable within safety bounds: Applications can restrict HTML further but not weaken security

Contribution Paths

Developers and researchers can contribute by: (1) testing for bypasses using `document.body.setHTML(evil)` on empty pages (security bounty eligible); (2) filing bug reports; (3) contributing to the web platform test suite; (4) participating in open specification questions on GitHub; (5) improving the JavaScript polyfill.

Key Takeaway

Braun emphasizes: "Use the right HTML parser before, after, and in the middle." By integrating sanitization into the browser's actual HTML parser with proper context, the Sanitizer API avoids double-parsing pitfalls that have plagued external sanitizer libraries. This represents a fundamental shift toward making the browser itself responsible for a core security property.",
```
